Anti-pollution construction ban in Capital forces migrant workers to return home
 Updated - November 07, 2026 10:14 pm IST 
 Shrimansi Kaushik READ LATER 
 SEE ALL 
 Remove 
 NEW DELHI, 27/06/2026: A view of the Delhi Development Authority (DDA) building. The housing complex being constructed to rehabilitate residents of the Kathputli Colony slum in West Delhi’s Shadipur was renamed as Pragati Apartments, in the Capital on Saturday. June 27, 2026. Photo: SHIV KUMAR PUSHPAKAR / The Hindu (To go with Suruchi Kumari's story)
 | Photo Credit: SHIV KUMAR PUSHPAKAR
 The implementation of Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) to curb rising air pollution in the Capital has brought construction activity to a halt, forcing hundreds of migrant workers to return to their native states or seek alternative employment during the winter months.
 The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) on Friday imposed a ban on dust-generating construction and demolition activities across the National Capital Region (NCR) and adjoining areas, with exemptions for essential public infrastructure projects, including metro, railway and healthcare facilities. The restrictions came into force as Delhi’s Air Quality Index (AQI) deteriorated to the ‘severe’ category.
 With construction sites shut, workers at labour chowks across the city have been left with little choice but to return home or look for alternative sources of income.
 Bimala Kumari, a construction worker from Etah in Uttar Pradesh, has had to rely on friends working as domestic helps to find employment for the winter months. She is now working as a domestic worker.
 “We have been told by the contractor that there will be no work until February. We were unaware of the pollution-related restrictions before coming to Delhi two months ago,” she said.
 Kumari migrated to Delhi with her three daughters and her sister’s family. “I am now working as a domestic help, hoping to support my daughters,” she said.
 Tabrez, a construction worker from Shakarpur, East Delhi, said his contractor had asked workers to look for alternative employment on the first day of the restrictions, November 2.
 “I work on a private plot, and the contractor informed all the workers that construction would remain suspended until January 31. Many have already left for their hometowns,” he said.
 Tabrez has since returned to his native village in Bihar.
 Manoj Kumar, another construction worker at Shahbad Dairy in North Delhi said his recent conversation with his contractor had yielded no clarity on employment prospects for the next two months.
 “GRAP has been enforced in previous years as well, but we would usually find work at alternative sites. This year, the restrictions appear to have been implemented more strictly. The site at Delhi University’s North Campus has also been closed. Initially, our contractor asked us to wait until November 20, but now it seems there will be no work until January 31,” he said.
 While the CAQM has imposed restrictions under GRAP Stages II and III across Delhi-NCR, subject to certain exemptions, the Delhi government had separately announced a ban on all construction and demolition activities in the Capital from November 5 to 20.
 Workers who had hoped to find employment in neighbouring areas such as Gautam Buddh Nagar and Faridabad have now found those options drying up as well.
 “My contractor was looking for work in Ghaziabad after telling us on November 3 that there would be no work until November 20. But now even that possibility is gone. I do not know any other trade, as I have worked in this sector all my life,” said the 48-year-old worker.
 His family of five is currently dependent on his wife’s earnings as a domestic worker and the income from a small grocery and snacks shop he runs from home.
 The restrictions have also caused difficulties for homeowners who had ongoing construction projects.
 Mukesh Kumar, a resident of Mahavir Enclave in South-West Delhi, had hired a contractor a month ago to rebuild his house from scratch.
 “The contractor had taken an advance equivalent to a month’s expenses to pay the labourers and procure materials. This is a major setback for me, as I had moved into a rented apartment with my family while the house was being rebuilt,” he said.
 However, some workers see the break in construction activity as an opportunity to return to their villages and spend time with their families.
 “Construction causes a lot of pollution. In a way, it is good that work has been halted. We do not earn during these months, but at least we are spared some exposure to the city’s polluted air,” said Jehangir, a worker from Purnea in Bihar.
 “The restrictions also give us an excuse to go home, visit our families and take care of things in the village,” he added.
